content: Podiatry, also known as podiatric medicine or chiropody, is a specialized field of healthcare that focuses on diagnosing, treating, and managing disorders of the foot, ankle, knee, leg, and hip, collectively referred to as the lower extremity. The scope of practice for podiatrists varies depending on the regulations of the country, state, or province in which they practice. Podiatrists, chiropodists, and podiatric surgeons are the professionals who provide care in this field. Historical Background The care of feet dates back to ancient Egypt, as evidenced by carvings in Ankmahor's tomb, which depict work on hands and feet. This suggests that foot care was an established practice throughout Egyptian civilization. Hippocrates, the ancient Greek physician, described corns and calluses and emphasized the importance of reducing hard skin and addressing the underlying causes. He invented skin scrapers, which were precursors to modern scalpels. The Roman scientist Aulus Cornelius Celsus is credited with naming corns, while Paul of Aegina, a Byzantine physician, provided detailed descriptions of corns and their treatment. Until the early 20th century, chiropodists (now called podiatrists) operated independently of organized medicine. They were licensed to treat foot and ankle conditions. Lewis Durlacher was among the first to advocate for a regulated profession, attempting to establish an association in 1854. Historical records show that notable figures, such as Napoleon and President Abraham Lincoln, employed chiropodists for foot care. In the United States, the first society of chiropodists was founded in New York in 1895, followed by the establishment of the first podiatry school in 1911. Similar developments occurred in the UK and Australia, with professional associations and training programs emerging in the early 20th century. The Role of a Podiatrist A podiatrist, also known as a foot doctor, is a healthcare professional specializing in the study and treatment of foot, ankle, and lower extremity disorders. The term podiatrist originated in the United States and is now widely used in English-speaking countries. In the UK, the titles podiatrist and chiropodist are protected and can only be used by individuals registered with the Health Professions Council. Podiatrists in the UK typically focus on non-invasive treatments but may perform minor surgical procedures, such as nail surgery under local anesthesia. In contrast, podiatrists in the United States have broader surgical privileges, including complex foot and ankle surgeries. Podiatry in Australia In Australia, podiatry is classified as an allied health profession. Practitioners must be licensed by their respective state boards. Australian podiatrists complete a 3to 4-year undergraduate degree, with the first two years focusing on biomedical sciences and the latter years on podiatry-specific subjects, such as biomechanics, orthopedics, pharmacology, and surgical techniques. Podiatric surgeons undergo additional training, including a master's degree and a surgical fellowship, before qualifying for advanced surgical practice. Prescribing rights for podiatrists vary by state, with some states allowing qualified practitioners to prescribe certain medications. Podiatry in Canada In Canada, the practice of podiatry varies by province. In British Columbia, Alberta, and Quebec, podiatrists are trained to the Doctor of Podiatric Medicine (DPM) level, similar to the United States. In Ontario, however, chiropodists and podiatrists are distinct professions, with chiropodists having a more limited scope of practice. The Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières established Canada's first podiatric medicine program in 2004. Podiatry in New Zealand Podiatry became a registered profession in New Zealand in 1969, with a three-year training program. The title chiropody was later replaced with podiatry, and the New Zealand School of Podiatry was established in 1970. Over time, the profession expanded its scope to include minor surgical procedures, such as ingrown toenail surgery, and the use of local anesthesia. By 1989, podiatrists were licensed to take X-rays, and diagnostic radiography became part of the degree curriculum. Podiatry in the United Kingdom In the UK, podiatrists specialize in the assessment, diagnosis, and treatment of foot and lower limb conditions. Their scope of practice includes managing high-risk patients, treating sports injuries, performing foot and nail surgeries, and educating patients on foot health. Podiatrists must be registered with the Health Professions Council to practice. The Society of Chiropodists and Podiatrists is the largest professional body representing podiatrists in the UK. Podiatry in the United States In the United States, podiatric medicine is practiced by licensed Doctors of Podiatric Medicine (DPM). Education involves a four-year podiatric medical school program, followed by a twoor three-year residency. Podiatric training emphasizes foot, ankle, and lower extremity conditions, with less focus on other medical areas. Podiatrists are trained in both medical and surgical treatments and can perform procedures ranging from nail care to complex reconstructive surgeries. Board certification is available in primary podiatric medicine, podiatric orthopedics, and podiatric surgery. Distinction from Orthopedic Foot and Ankle Surgery Orthopedic foot and ankle surgeons complete a medical degree (MD or DO) followed by a 5to 6-year residency in orthopedic surgery, with limited time dedicated to foot and ankle surgery. Some orthopedic surgeons pursue additional fellowships in foot and ankle surgery. In contrast, podiatric surgeons undergo 2to 3-year residencies focused exclusively on foot and ankle surgery. While there is some overlap in practice, podiatrists are considered experts in foot and ankle care. Specialties and Subfields Podiatrists may specialize in various areas, including: Pediatric foot conditions (Podopaediatrics) Sports medicine Diabetic foot care and wound management Forensic podiatry Rheumatology Gerontology Reconstructive foot and ankle surgery Minimally invasive surgery Professional Organizations Podiatrists are supported by various professional societies, including: American Podiatric Medical Association (APMA) American Board of Podiatric Surgery Australasian College of Podiatric Surgeons Society of Chiropodists and Podiatrists (UK) Career Outlook The demand for podiatrists is expected to grow steadily. In the United States, the median salary for podiatrists was $150,000 in 2006. Podiatrists often work in solo practices, group practices, or multidisciplinary clinics. They may also provide care in nursing homes, hospitals, or government healthcare systems. Educational Institutions There are eight colleges of podiatric medicine in the United States, governed by the American Association of Colleges of Podiatric Medicine (AACPM). These institutions provide comprehensive training in podiatric medicine and surgery, preparing graduates for diverse career opportunities in the field.
